subtype: Colleague who starts but does not close [Receiver]
passage: Team lead's note, Friday. I'm Asif, and this week I watched how Parul spends the evenings. Manav starts tasks with real energy: the vendor list, the price comparison, the customer follow-up. Each one is left about eighty percent finished. Parul has been quietly chasing the vendors, correcting the price sheet and sending the follow-up mails, and twice stayed until eight. Parul did not complain, only said, “It's fine, it needs doing.” Manav has no idea this is happening. What I did next: I asked at Monday's meeting who owns each task until it is closed, and wrote a name beside every line. Then I told Parul privately that the evenings would not be covered again.

qa.q: Until what time did Parul stay on two evenings?
qa.a: Parul stayed until eight on two evenings.

qa.q: What might Parul be feeling behind “It's fine, it needs doing”?
qa.a: Parul is probably tired and quietly resentful but unwilling to make a fuss, and feels responsible for the tasks getting done.

qa.q: What did Asif change at Monday's meeting?
qa.a: Asif asked who owns each task until it is closed and wrote a name beside every line, so loose ends no longer fall to Parul by default.

qa.q: How might Manav see the situation?
qa.a: Manav has no idea the loose ends are being closed by someone else, so Manav probably feels the tasks are progressing well.

grounding: A team relies on someone who starts tasks brightly and leaves loose ends, and another person quietly pays the cost.

subtype: Colleague who starts but does not close [Receiver]
passage: Thursday. Another late one. Uma is wonderful at starting things: yesterday she launched the new event checklist with such energy that everyone was excited. By afternoon it had six open items: two suppliers not confirmed, the seating list incomplete, one invitation unsent. I noticed them because I had promised the client an update. So I called the suppliers, finished the list and sent the invitation, which took my whole evening. Nobody has asked me to. I don't want to complain about Uma, because she's not lazy and the ideas are good. But my own work slid to tomorrow, and I keep feeling a low hum of resentment I don't quite want. Maybe the checklist needs a name against each item. — Darshan

qa.q: How many open items did the checklist have by afternoon?
qa.a: The checklist had six open items by afternoon.

qa.q: What feeling is Darshan carrying that Darshan does not quite want?
qa.a: Darshan feels a low hum of resentment, mixed with reluctance to blame Uma.

qa.q: What could Darshan do next to stop the pattern?
qa.a: Suggest that each checklist item has a name against it and a closing date, and raise it kindly with Uma or the team.

qa.q: How might Uma see the checklist she started?
qa.a: Uma probably feels proud of launching it with energy and may not know that the open items have become Darshan's work.

grounding: Someone who starts brightly and leaves loose ends creates unseen work that another person quietly finishes.
